title: Senior's toolkit: automated refactorings and safe history
summary: IDE refactorings with their shortcuts, snapshot tests that lock behaviour, and the git commands that keep a refactor reviewable.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: automated refactorings and safe history
steps.body: Refactoring at work means many small, safe moves: lock the current behaviour, let the IDE do the mechanical edits it cannot get wrong, commit each step on its own, and know how to find the commit that changed behaviour if one slips through.

toolkit.what: Select lines and turn them into a named method. The IDE works out the parameters and return value, so nothing is missed.
flags: Rider (Rider/IntelliJ keymap; its Visual Studio keymap uses the Visual Studio keys)
toolkit.example: Select the 12 lines under // apply discounts, Ctrl+R,Ctrl+M, name it ApplyDiscounts

toolkit.what: Turn a hard-coded value or a hidden dependency inside a method into a parameter, and update every caller in one go.
flags: Visual Studio / VS Code: Introduce parameter for ...
Rider (Rider keymap): Change Signature (add, remove, reorder)
toolkit.example: Cursor on DateTime.Now inside IsOverdue, Ctrl+., Introduce parameter, name it now

toolkit.what: The reverse of extract: replace a variable or a one-line method with its body everywhere. Useful when a wrapper adds a name but no meaning.
flags: Visual Studio / VS Code (inline temporary variable, inline method)
toolkit.example: Cursor on var temp, Ctrl+., Inline temporary variable

toolkit.what: Delete a member or type only after checking nothing uses it, and offer to fix the usages. In Visual Studio, check with Shift+F12 first.
flags: Visual Studio / VS Code: confirm zero references

toolkit.what: Snapshot (characterization) tests with the **Verify** library (`Verify.Xunit`, `Verify.NUnit`...). The first run saves the output; later runs fail on any difference. Lock legacy behaviour before you touch it.
flags: the approved snapshot, committed to git
replace the verified file with the received one, after reading the diff

toolkit.what: Stage a file hunk by hunk. Lets you commit a pure refactor separately from a behaviour change, so the reviewer can trust each commit.
flags: split the hunk into smaller ones
park unfinished work to start a clean refactor
toolkit.example: git add -p src/Orders/OrderProcessor.cs && git commit -m "Extract ApplyDiscounts (no behaviour change)"

toolkit.what: Binary search through history for the commit that broke something. With a test command, git finds it on its own.
flags: begin, mark the current commit bad, mark a known good one
let a command decide: exit 0 is good, non-zero is bad
finish and go back to where you were
toolkit.example:
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good v1.4.0
git bisect run dotnet test --filter "FullyQualifiedName~InvoiceTotals"
git bisect reset

steps.prompt: Match each shortcut to the refactoring it runs.
pairs: the quick-actions menu, where VS Code lists its refactorings

steps.prompt: Invoice totals are off by one cent for some orders. It was fine at the `v1.4.0` tag, and there are 120 commits since. A test `InvoiceTotals_RoundsHalfUp` now fails. What is the fastest way to find the commit that broke it?
options: `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good v1.4.0`, then `git bisect run dotnet test --filter "FullyQualifiedName~InvoiceTotals"`
Read the 120 commit messages and guess
Revert the last ten commits one at a time
steps.explain: Bisect halves the range each step: about 7 test runs for 120 commits, and `run` does them unattended. `git blame` only shows the last change to each line, which may not be the one that broke the rounding.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a safe refactor of a legacy method in order.
lines: Write a Verify snapshot test over real sample input and approve the snapshot
Extract method on the first block, using the IDE refactoring
Run the tests: the snapshot must still match
git add -p and commit with a message saying no behaviour change

items: A 120-line method with three commented sections
The same 8 lines appear in two branches
A method whose only line calls another method with the same arguments
`IsOverdue()` reads `DateTime.Now` inside and is hard to test
A tax rate of `0.2m` is hard-coded but differs per country

steps.prompt: Your branch renames 40 methods **and** fixes a rounding bug. The reviewer says the diff is impossible to read. What should you have done?
options: Commit the refactor and the fix separately (`git add -p` helps split a file), so each commit is either "no behaviour change" or one small fix
Squash everything into one commit with a long message
Leave out the tests so the diff is smaller
Do the renames by hand so they show up as fewer changes
steps.explain: A pure refactor commit can be reviewed quickly because the tests prove nothing changed. Mixing it with a fix hides the one line that matters among hundreds that do not.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before touching legacy code, lock what it does with a snapshot test. Then let the IDE do every mechanical edit, run the tests after each one, and commit refactors on their own. When something breaks anyway, `git bisect run` finds the commit while you get a coffee.
